en: The Sutra on the Samādhi of the Tathāgata Ratna, Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jīvaka from India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, together with twelve hundred [monks].
There was an assembly of one hundred and fifty bhikṣus and ninety billion bodhisattvas, all of whom were just like Mañjuśrī!

At that time, throughout the kingdom of Rājagṛha and the surrounding areas of the Bamboo Grove—extending upward to the thirty-six heavens and downward to the infinite lands of the Buddha-fields—all produced *mandārava* flowers.
There were nine trillion varieties of these flowers, each of a different color, surpassing the brilliance of this world; each flower had a million petals, and upon every petal sat a Tathāgata.
Everywhere there were canopies made of ten thousand jewels interlaced together; atop each canopy, the sounds of ten thousand kinds of music played for mutual enjoyment.
Before each Buddha stood a bodhisattva, such as the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and others, inquiring about the Dharma.

At that time, the ground of the Bamboo Grove became entirely level, like the buddha-field of Samantabhadra; throughout this trichiliocosm, the realms of all the Buddhas of the suns and moons were completely eclipsed by its radiance, such that no light remained visible.

At that time, within the realms of all Buddhas, the great hells were entirely stilled; their poisonous pains and arduous sufferings ceased to exist, and all attained peace and security. For a hundred days, they were all able to behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, the beasts and birds all went without food for a hundred days, listening only to the flavor of the Dharma;
they were unaware of themselves as sentient beings, yet they also beheld the Buddha.

At that time, among the people of the kingdom of Rājagṛha, none for a hundred days again consumed the five flavors; all took the Dharma as their flavor and all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Within the realm of the Buddha of this trichiliocosm, the trees spontaneously produced music, and they naturally entertained one another.
At that time, the Bamboo Grove was transformed into a pond, within which were a hundred thousand varieties of lotuses as large as small mountains.
Each flower had four hundred thousand petals, and upon every petal there was a lion throne covered with a lattice of pearls.
Upon each seat sat a bodhisattva, such as Mañjuśrī, and before each seat stood a celestial attendant bodhisattva.

Within the jeweled lattice canopies, ten thousand kinds of music played for their mutual enjoyment; trees that had withered and died for a thousand years all burst forth into bloom, and the trees throughout the trichiliocosm buddha-field all bent their branches toward one another from the four directions.
At that time, at the site where the Buddha taught in the Bamboo Grove, all the women were transformed into men; free from desire, they all attained the Dharma-eye.
Thereupon, the Buddha entered the Samādhi of the Tathāgata Vast Manifestation of Jewels, whereby nine hundred million buddha-fields were immediately shaken.

At that time, within this samādhi, nothing at all was relinquished. From the infinite Buddha-fields of the eastern direction, countless bodhisattvas—each equal to a Tathāgata—arrived, each holding formless flowers and one hundred thousand varieties of flowers of diverse colors. They came to the Bamboo Grove, paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, scattered the flowers over the Perfectly Awakened One, and withdrew to their seats.

Furthermore, from the infinite Buddha-lands of the southern direction, another countless number of bodhisattvas—each equal to a Tathāgata—arrived, each holding two hundred thousand varieties of flowers. They came to the Bamboo Grove, paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, scattered the flowers over the Perfectly Awakened One, and withdrew to sit.

Furthermore, from the infinite Buddha-fields of the West, each dispatched countless bodhisattvas, all equal to the Tathāgatas, who each brought three hundred thousand varieties of flowers of diverse colors. They came to the Bamboo Grove, paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, scattered the flowers over the assembly, and withdrew to their seats.

Furthermore, from the infinite Buddha-fields of the North, there were likewise dispatched countless bodhisattvas, all equal to the Tathāgatas, who each brought four hundred thousand varieties of flowers of diverse colors. They came to the Bamboo Grove, paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, scattered the flowers over the assembly, and withdrew to their seats.

Furthermore, from the buddha-field in the eastern corner, countless bodhisattvas were dispatched, all equal to the Tathāgata; each holding formless flowers, they arrived at the Bamboo Grove, paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, scattered the flowers over the Buddha and the assembly, and withdrew to sit.

Furthermore, from the buddha-field in the southern corner, countless bodhisattvas were likewise dispatched, all equal to the Tathāgata; each holding flowers free from conceptual desire, they arrived at the Bamboo Grove, paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, scattered the flowers over the Perfectly Awakened One and the great assembly, and withdrew to sit.

Furthermore, from the innumerable Buddha-fields in the western corner, countless bodhisattvas—each equal to a Tathāgata—were dispatched; each holding a "soundless" flower, they arrived at the Bamboo Grove, paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, scattered flowers over the Buddha and the great assembly, and withdrew to sit.

Furthermore, from the infinite Buddha-fields in the northern corner, countless bodhisattvas—each equal to a Tathāgata—were dispatched; each holding a *māndārava* flower, they arrived at the Bamboo Grove, paid homage to the Buddha, scattered flowers upon the Buddha and the gathered assembly, and withdrew to sit.

Furthermore, from the infinite Buddha-fields of the upper direction, each dispatched countless bodhisattvas, all equal to the Tathāgata, each holding flowers of variegated colors. They came to the Bamboo Grove, paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, scattered the flowers over the Perfectly Awakened One and the great assembly, and withdrew to sit.

From the infinite Buddha-fields of the lower direction, each likewise dispatched countless bodhisattvas, all equal to the Tathāgata, each holding various exquisite flowers. They came to the Bamboo Grove, paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, scattered the flowers over the Perfectly Awakened One and the great assembly, and withdrew to sit.

The various devas of the upper realms, whose merit from past lives was most sublime, encountered the Buddha’s great assembly and the samādhi of the Tathāgata Vast and Great Treasure, each adorning themselves individually.
The sons of the gods in the heavens were all caused to first resolve their minds [for enlightenment].
Brahmā, leading countless devas, each held celestial incense and celestial flowers;
furthermore, the devas of the Mahābrahmā assembly, leading countless devas, each held various celestial flowers and incense.
The Śubhakṛtsna devas held non-worldly celestial flowers;
all the noble devas held celestial music and stood in the void to perform it.
For a hundred days, day and night, the entire trichiliocosm was filled with the sound of the Dharma as they experienced this, and they came to the Bamboo Grove to pay homage to the Buddha.

The Devaputra Priya further led countless devaputras, each holding celestial musical instruments, to the Bamboo Grove to pay homage to the Buddha, while providing entertainment for the devas in mid-air.
The devas of the Kāyika heaven held thousands of millions of kinds of blended incense and scattered it over the Buddha and the bodhisattvas, prostrating themselves before the Buddha.
All the devas from throughout the heavens came together to assemble within the Bamboo Grove.
Reaching upward to the thirty-six heavens without interruption, there were entirely devaputras.
The great nāga kings, each leading countless retinues, held flowers that those in the human world could not obtain and rained them down upon the Bamboo Grove.
The asura kings, each likewise leading countless retinues, each held various flowers and rained them down upon the Buddha and the bodhisattvas.
The various garuḍas each brought their own countless retinues and arrived at the Bamboo Grove;
the various kinnaras each brought their own countless retinues and arrived at the Bamboo Grove;
the various mahoragas also brought their retinues and arrived at the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Buddha manifested the *Ratna-tathāgata-samādhi*, whereby nine hundred million buddha-fields were immediately shaken.
Seeing the earth tremble violently, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now all the bodhisattvas, devas, and people from distant regions have assembled, extending upward as far as the thirty-six heavens."
The earth shook violently;
what is the significance of this?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The response that is non-responsive is its true response.
Śāriputra again addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“What is this ‘response that is non-responsive,’ and what kind of thing is it?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If your doubts are not severed, go to where the Bodhisattva of the Tathāgata Ratna is.
Śāriputra adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Tathāgata several times, and with palms joined, addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
"Today, from the ten directions above up to the thirty-six heavens, hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas from Buddha-fields have all assembled. What kind of response is this?
We pray that the Tathāgata will explain it."
The Tathāgata said to Śāriputra:
"If you were an Arhat, would you have come here to resolve what was originally such a heavy doubt?
The Tathāgata-Bodhisattva said:
“Śāriputra! If there were always the perception of existence, such perception would not be the work of cessation; rather, it is without perception and without action.
For this reason, the Tathāgata Ratnadharmas proclaimed to Śāriputra:

"When I first resolved my mind [on enlightenment], I sought the path of a bodhisattva together with thirty-six billion people; at the time of my perfect awakening, they were all among them, yet none of them arose the thought, 'I shall not do it.'"

All things are entirely non-self and empty; all phenomena are without self, and there is no seeking for birth and death. Birth and death have no path, nor is there anyone who cuts it off; space has no master, and the "self" is not something that exists as a manifest phenomenon.

It is like a mirage, arising and acting without marks; to maintain such constructed phenomena, to extinguish conduct while seeking vows, and to harbor the desire to attain them—this is to carry a heavy burden.

Regarding the clarity of their transgressions: they claim for themselves that they have attained the Way, yet they give rise to conceptualizations of attainment and conceptualizations of transgression; they destroy all wisdom while seeking the Three Honored Ones, and from these conceptualizations they seek to grasp *nirvāṇa*. They believe that with the exhaustion of doubt, the body will be extinguished;

however, birth and death are not severed, and they claim to have attained the *nirvāṇa* of an Arhat. It is like a person whose life has ended lying upon a bed: for a moment they hear of it and obtain a brief rest, yet though their life has ended, they have not yet left the body.
"Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas attain dhyāna for themselves; is this not a great accumulation of doubt?
The Tathāgata said to Śāriputra:
"The question you have asked is indeed such."
The Tathāgata said to Śāriputra:
"Do you see when a dragon intends to send rain and raises clouds?
Śāriputra replied:

"Looking at it from all four sides, one cannot discern where the clouds come from; how much less can one discern the path by which a bodhisattva comes, when that bodhisattva has attained all sixty thousand samādhis from the ninth stage downward? Where does such a bodhisattva come from?"
Śāriputra addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
"With wisdom such as this, the knots of doubt within my mind have now been entirely destroyed; there is no longer any root of doubt remaining."

Originally, I had not attained the learning; it was only through meeting a virtuous friend that I have now severed and extinguished my own [self-centered] intentions, so as not to escape the Wheel of Dharma, yet to ensure that the root of my doubt is never severed.
Now, hearing the Venerable One’s Dharma brings me no benefit.
It is like playing music for a hundred birds; there would be no one at all who could hear or understand it.

In this same way, it is only for the sake of the newly resolved Mahāsattvas seated here that the gods and humans of this great assembly are enabled to hear this sublime samādhi—how truly majestic and profound it is!

"One should simply draw near to the Honored One. However, because in my previous lives I did not encounter virtuous friends, I was unable to see this samādhi and the wisdom of the Tathāgata; thus, the doubts in my mind have now been dispelled.
It is like a place in darkness that is momentarily illuminated by fire; when the fire is extinguished, the darkness returns. Now, having heard this, it is just so for me."
Śāriputra joined his palms and addressed the Tathāgata, saying:

“I now beg to create a great fire eight thousand *li* in extent, reaching upward to the thirty-six heavens; may I place my body within it for billions of *kalpas*, and thereafter emerge again only to enter the three evil realms and be devoured by the people of the world.”

After thousands of billions of kalpas, one is born as a human being and serves a great man like a slave; if one seeks a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and attains them, can the wishes in my heart be fulfilled?
The Tathāgata truly said:

"Even a great fire that rises as high as the thirty-six heavens can still be extinguished by pouring water upon it; however, if one's original resolve is feeble and one lacks the profound realization of the root of merit, one shall not attain *samyaksambodhi*."
"It is simply because they did not attain *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and did not encounter virtuous friends that they have not reached this state!
Having finished his inquiry on this matter, Śāriputra returned to his seat.
The Tathāgata adjusted his robes and paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, saying:
"I wish to ask a question. The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!
You should ask.
Thus addressed, the Tathāgata spoke to the Buddha:
"All dharmas are without a master; who is it that achieves omniscience (sarvajñatā)?
Who is it that achieves perfect enlightenment?
Who is it that achieves arhatship or pratyekabuddhahood?"
"I pray that the Tathāgata will, for the sake of the Mahāsattvas in this assembly, distinguish and explain their respective attainments of certainty.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
The Tathāgata now wishes to sever the great root of birth and death throughout the ten directions.
If there are good sons or good daughters who desire to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should practice the nine dharmas of the jewels.
What are the nine treasures of the Dharma?
First, seeing that the various devas have no actual location and exist as names alone;
second, seeing that the people of the world exist as mere words alone.
The Three Jewels are merely the accumulation of suffering within the diligent toil of the five destinies!
The Four Jewels—water, fire, wind, and earth—are merely playthings!
As for the fifth, the future, the past, and the present are like the plantain tree, devoid of thought.
Sixth, to manifest that birth and death have no original limit.
Seventh, to contemplate all samādhis as being tranquil and devoid of coming or going.
Eighth, one should contemplate the suns, moons, and buddha-fields of the trichiliocosm, seeing them clearly such that no one attains samādhi.
"Ninth, seeing the sentient beings moving about within the suns and moons of the trichiliocosm, one desires to deliver them all so that they may become equal to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the Tathāgata:
"One who attains this thought of non-action can decisively sever the great conceptualizations regarding the ten directions."
The Tathāgata again addressed the Perfectly Awakened One, saying:
“Since all dharmas are not known through conceptual perception, by abiding in what manner should one attain the dharma of non-abiding?”
The Buddha said:
“That all dharmas have no abiding is itself a conceptualization;

that there is no arising of thought is likewise a conceptualization. To think that neither conceptualization nor the Path exists is also a conceptualization; to strive to bring about their cessation is likewise a conceptualization.”
The Tathāgata addressed the Deva among Devas, saying:
"By what means should one deliver those who desire?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is because of such questions as those asked by the Tathāgata that this is not within the reach of arhats or pratyekabuddhas.”

All desires are stainless; all desires have no crossing over; all desires have no master; all desires have no comers or goers; all desires are like space, such that nothing can obscure or conceal them; they are equal to nirvāṇa and equal to the nameless.
When the Tathāgata had finished his inquiry, he paid homage to the God among Gods and withdrew to sit.
Pañcaśikha addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Today this great assembly of bodhisattvas desires to stand beneath the Bodhi tree, desires to attain the state of non-arising, and desires to adorn thousands of billions of buddha-fields. They desire to instruct the ten directions so that all the buddha-fields of the ten directions shall each become like this present assembly in the Bamboo Grove."
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!
The question posed by the Bodhisattva Pañcaśikha is most profound, most profound.”
The Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattva Pañcaśikha, saying:
“If you wish to cause the great assemblies of the ten directions to sit beneath the Bodhi tree;
if you wish to establish them in the state of non-arising;”
If you wish to adorn all Buddha-fields;

if you wish to instruct and receive [the teachings] throughout the ten directions, so that all Buddha-fields may each assemble together just as they have assembled today in this Bamboo Grove, you should practice the Eightfold Right Path.
First, it is directly the resonance of the nameless.
Second, it is directly the sound of the nameless.
Third, it is directly observing that the Buddha-fields of the ten directions are non-dual.
Fourth, to see that the dharmas of the three thousand great thousandfold world systems are all equally signless and detached.
Fifth, to directly contemplate all things in the ten directions with the desire to make them equal to the Buddha.
Sixth, being straightforward regarding the Dharma without forming mental constructs, they see that all things neither arise nor perish.
Seventh, whatever they perceive with straightforwardness entirely enters into various samādhis, wherein they store their thoughts within the signless retribution of non-abiding.
Eighth, one directly perceives the Buddhas of the ten directions, such that nirvāṇa and non-nirvāṇa are likewise entirely equal.
These are the eight rectitudes.
A Bodhisattva who practices according to the Dharma will swiftly attain the dharma of non-arising.
"From this, one obtains instruction regarding all Buddha-fields;
from this, one swiftly attains a great assembly such as the Bamboo Grove assembly of today.
The Tathāgata again addressed the Perfectly Awakened One, saying:
"Today those from afar have all come together to assemble at the Bamboo Grove and have all been able to see the Buddha.
As it is thus, they have each rejoiced so much that they have not eaten for several days. Each person spoke thus to themselves.
All the bodhisattvas, devas, and human beings were able to see the Buddha and behold all the samādhis.
Is this brought about by their original vows?
The Buddha should explain this for the sake of the mahāsattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!

What the Tathāgata has asked is most profound; you wish to act as such a bridge for all the bodhisattvas gathered here, as well as for the devas, humans, and others who have newly resolved their minds.”
The Buddha said to the Tathāgata:
"These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, devas, humans, great nāga kings, and kṣetrapāla kings who have all gathered at Zhūyuán today, have all heard and seen these samādhis;
yet this was not their original vow, nor were they separated from their original vow."

In all his conduct he is ever diligent, never losing the various samādhis, nor losing his spiritual friends; life after life he remains distant from worldly affairs, remaining in profound stillness and seldom gathering in assemblies. He desires only this samādhi; therefore, I now use these precious *vajra-nirvāṇa* pearls to rain down upon this great assembly!
The Tathāgata addressed the Perfectly Awakened One, saying:
"In this assembly there are mahāsattvas who have newly resolved their minds and wish to practice this samādhi; by what means should they attain it?"
The Buddha, the Tathāgata, said:
"Your question is most excellent.
If a Mahāsattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment wishes to practice this samādhi, they should practice eight precious dharmas."
What are the eight treasures of the Dharma?
First, this samādhi right before the Buddha—this is the first treasure of the Dharma.

Second, the treasure of the Dharma is to make offerings to all the arhats of the ten directions, following them for billions upon billions of kalpas, hearing and understanding this [samādhi] all at once, and remaining close to the honored samādhi without distance; this is the second treasure of the Dharma.

Third, making offerings to the śarīra [relics], filling the space from the earth up to the thirty-sixth heaven without any gaps, yet realizing that this alone does not provide ultimate benefit; instead, turning one's mind toward practice and inquiring about wisdom—this is the third of the Three Jewels.

The four Dharma-jewels are: attaining the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*), and not being separated from the ten directions throughout birth and death; these are the four Dharma-jewels. The five Dharma-jewels are:

when a bodhisattva perceives the suffering of the five realms of existence, his mind desires to bring them all to rest and deliver them; he saves their lives with his own body and does not consider it a laborious toil, seeking only to cause them to attain Buddhahood; these are the five Dharma-jewels.

Regarding the six dharmas of the Jewel: when a bodhisattva serves the people of the ten directions throughout the world, they always act as a servant serving a master; they do not seek to deliver them by treating themselves as noble while making others suffer. Why is this so?
Knowing that the root is sought through non-existence, because the root has no arising—these are the six dharma-jewels.

As for the seventh dharma-jewel: when a bodhisattva observes the ninety-six kinds of external paths and, within them, becomes aware of their desire to give rise to conceptualizations, grasp at dharmas, and dwell therein—this is the seventh dharma-jewel.

Regarding the eightfold jewel of the Dharma: practicing the six pāramitās and making offerings to the community of bhikṣus for billions of kalpas is not equal to hearing this Jewel Tathāgata Samādhi even for a single moment.
Regarding those in the ten directions who shall become Buddhas, by what shall they be certified?
Those who hear of this Jewel Tathāgata Samādhi are the people of the ten directions who have attained the certification of Buddhahood.
If one has newly resolved their mind toward this samādhi and joyfully understands it, this is equivalent to having understood ten million samādhis and having already attained the Tathāgata Samādhi.
"These are the eight dharma-jewels that cause one to practice this samādhi; by doing so, one may attain the gates of dhāraṇī.
When the Tathāgata had finished answering these questions, he returned to his seat and smiled.
Mañjuśrī adjusted his robes, prostrated with his head to the ground, and with palms joined, paid homage to the Buddha, saying to him:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; since you have smiled, there must be a meaning behind it. I pray that the Buddha will explain it."
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“The buddha-field from which the Tathāgata Ratna has come is beyond nine hundred million buddha-fields; that field is named Sarvadharmasvabhāva-anirveda-aviṣādita.”

When good sons and good daughters go there, they are not born from a womb, nor are they born through suffering, nor are they born through affectionate attachment; they all arise and immediately stand firm within hundreds of billions of various fragrant flowers.
There are always sounds of chaotic music for them to enjoy morning and evening, yet these are performed solely as music of the unconditioned Dharma and solely as music of the tranquil Dharma.

If a son or daughter of good family hears of this samādhi, they shall immediately retrogress six hundred and forty kalpas [of suffering]. When their transgressions are exhausted and their lives end, they will attain rebirth; those who are so reborn take delight solely in all the various samādhis.
In the realm of the Tathāgata Ratna, there is no light from the sun or moon; although they exist, they do not manifest.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who are reborn there, the light of the sun, moon, and stars will immediately appear for them. For those who are destined to be reborn through this samādhi, the light of the stars, sun, and moon shall all be seen.
The Buddhas of the ten directions said,
"Today he has again been reborn in the realm of the Tathāgata Ratna.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions then asked the Buddhas of the ten directions:
"What serves as proof?
The Buddhas of the ten directions replied,
"We take the luminous appearance of the stars, the moon, and the sun as our proof."

"The number of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas is such that it cannot be known by any Arhat or Pratyekabuddha; only the sons and daughters of good family, as well as Bodhisattvas, who have been reborn in that land, know it themselves!"
"This is why I smile.
Subhūti and Śāriputra, the two foremost among the worthy ones, rose, touched their heads to the ground, and paid homage to the Perfectly Awakened One, saying:
"We pray that the Buddha will bestow great grace upon us and extend his vast compassion toward us."

"By means of the Buddha's majestic spiritual power and his supernormal faculties granted to us, we wish to go to the land of the Tathāgata Ratna, the realm where all dharmas are spontaneous, to behold it, and then return in an instant."
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!
Then the Venerable Arhat Śāriputra and Subhūti, riding upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, arrived in an instant at the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratna.
He then again saw that the land of the Tathāgata Ratna was also like the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha during the assembly of Śākyamuni Buddha;
he saw countless bodhisattvas dispatched from the east, and innumerable bodhisattvas from the south, and so it was throughout the ten directions, up to the assemblies in the thirty-six heavens.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Did the Tathāgata follow me and others to arrive at this land?
Subhūti and Śāriputra returned to the Bamboo Grove in an instant, and the assembly was as it had been before.
The Buddha asked Śāriputra:
"Regarding the land of the Tathāgata Ratnadarśana that you have just observed, what is the nature of its people, and how many individuals did he instruct?
Subhūti and Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Behold that land; it is entirely like the present time when we are gathered here in the Bamboo Grove.
Śāriputra paid homage to the Buddha and said:
“The merit of the Buddha is most sublime; today, this great assembly of devas and humans has been able to see such brilliance as this.”
The Bodhisattva Samiti rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
You should ask.
Thus addressed, Samitra Bodhisattva said to the Buddha:
"Do phenomena that are unarisen possess perception or not?
Does a thought that has not yet arisen possess consciousness or not?
Is Nirvana, which is tranquil, existent or non-existent?"
Niyi said: "That which is neither arising nor having form or no-form is the teaching within that interval; as for the place where birth and death are established, who is the master?
That which creates emptiness by means of emptiness is the master."

When Samantabhadra heard the Buddha explain this matter in such a way, eighty-six thousand devas and humans immediately attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). They then remained in mid-air one hundred and sixty *zhang* above the ground, descended, and paid homage to the Buddha.
At that time, the sun and moon of this trichiliocosm shook violently once more. Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and asked the Buddha:
"Just now the earth shook greatly; what is the omen of this?"
The Buddha spoke to Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"The reason the earth shakes so greatly is not merely that this world-system moves; rather, all the buddha-fields of the ten directions likewise shake.
Furthermore, eighty-six thousand devas and humans in each of those fields have attained the dwelling in the dharma of non-arising, and thus abide in the void of space in this manner."
"For this reason, the great earth has merely trembled!
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying,
"From what cause does this arise?"
“There are six dharmas that one who has resolved [for enlightenment] should always maintain. What are the six?

The first dharma is: knowing the thirty-six heavens, those who are destined to attain Buddhahood but have not yet received their prediction (vyākaraṇa), I shall go to grant them that prediction, without sharing this knowledge with the people of the worlds throughout the ten directions.”

Regarding the second dharma: among the suns and moons of the trichiliocosm, whenever a son or daughter of good family is destined to attain Buddhahood, I shall go to all of them and bestow my prediction upon them, without sharing this knowledge with the people of the worlds in the ten directions.

Regarding the third dharma: as for those among the hundreds of thousands in the hells who are destined to attain Buddhahood, I shall go to all of them and bestow predictions upon them, without sharing this knowledge with the people of the worlds throughout the ten directions.

Regarding the four dharmas: as for the places where people throughout the ten directions will be reborn after their lives end, I know them all completely, whereas the people of the worlds throughout the ten directions do not know them together with me.

The fifth dharma is that when the lives of all people throughout the ten directions of the world come to an end, I know them all, yet I do not share this knowledge with the people of the ten directions.
The sixth dharma is that regarding whether the Buddhas of the ten directions shall enter parinirvāṇa or not enter parinirvāṇa, I do not share this knowledge with the people of the ten directions.
"These are the six dharmas of abiding;
from these, one quickly attains the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This samādhi is most sublime, most sublime. Now, I wish for all those gathered here to attain this samādhi; what dharmas should they practice?
The Buddha said:
"They should practice nine dharmas."
What are the nine?
The first dharma is to perceive all dharmas as entirely pure and boundless.
The second dharma is to perceive the heavens as entirely pure.
The third dharma is viewing all births and deaths as pure and boundless.
The fourth dharma is viewing the five destinies as entirely pure.
The fifth dharma is having no seeking within desire, being entirely pure.
The sixth dharma is to perceive all forms within the three realms as entirely pure and boundless.
The seventh dharma is to see all the hells as entirely pure and boundless.
The eighth dharma is to contemplate nirvana as entirely boundless.
As for the nine dharmas: there is no one throughout the ten directions who can utter their names.
These are the nine dharmas.
One who practices in this manner will swiftly attain this samādhi.
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When this teaching on the Tathāgata was spoken, I immediately attained sixty thousand samādhis. Do these samādhis have limits?
If one attains sixty thousand samādhis, does that constitute having limits?"
The Buddha said:
"Though you have attained sixty thousand samādhis, they are merely names;
you cannot yet reach the ultimate limit of fully possessing all samādhis."
The Buddha said:
"Samādhis are not limited to a single type; there is the samādhi of non-thought, and there is the samādhi of detachment from desire."
There is the samādhi of sitting and hearing the Buddhas of the ten directions;
there is the samādhi of adorning the buddha-fields with flowers and incense;
and there is the samādhi wherein all people to whom one preaches the Dharma return to their original state.
There is the samādhi of emerging from all desires with the thought of non-return;
there is the samādhi of manifesting a hundred kinds of musical sounds while preaching the sūtras;
and there is the samādhi wherein, when the Dharma is preached, flowers and incense from billions of koṭis of buddha-fields spontaneously arrive.
There is the samādhi for subduing all māras;
there is the samādhi for generating the lion-like mind to walk alone and stride forth;
and there is the samādhi by which, wherever one turns, one does not fail to generate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The samādhi wherein there is no place where one is not honored;
the samādhi wherein when a turbulent wind arises, it sounds like the voice of the Buddha preaching the sūtras;
the samādhi wherein there is no gate that does not open toward it.
There is the samādhi that manifests lion thrones wherever one dwells;
there is the samādhi of flying to the ten directions;
and there is the samādhi of the infinite coming and going of bodhisattvas through the gates toward the ten directions.
There is the samādhi of knowing the minds of people in the ten directions;
there is the samādhi of destroying and extinguishing all perceptions;
there is the samādhi of destroying and extinguishing all consciousnesses.
There is the samādhi that merges all the lands of the ten directions into a single land;
there is the samādhi of inexhaustible resolve;
and there is the samādhi of beholding the three realms and perceiving not a single person therein.
There is the samādhi of traveling from one buddha-field to another;
there is the samādhi of ensuring that the Dharma is never interrupted wherever one may be;
and there is the samādhi of constantly encountering the Buddha wherever one may be.
There is the samādhi wherein one sits and observes the great armies, great fires, great waters, and great winds of the ten directions without fear, remaining therein to instruct and transform others;
there is the samādhi wherein, wherever one may be, one takes the Dharma alone as one’s vessel;
and there is the samādhi of the thought of non-retrogression, which a good man or good woman attains immediately upon hearing these samādhis.
This samādhi is vast and immeasurable; therefore, he dwells in this great assembly to expound it.
"There is the samādhi called 'Nameless';
there is the samādhi called 'Abiding in All Dharmas'."
There is the samādhi of the various renowned wisdoms;
there is the samādhi of the teaching of the Dharma;
there is the samādhi that destroys and eliminates arhats and pratyekabuddhas.
There is the samādhi of the Dharma-treasure;
there is the samādhi of the dhāraṇī of the nameless dharma;
there is the samādhi of knowing the minds of others.
There is the samādhi of severing all afflictions;
there is the samādhi of restraining the power of sensual desires and thoughts;
there is the samādhi of the ten powers.
There is the samādhi of wisdom;
there is the samādhi of the sphere of activity of light;
there is the samādhi of the incalculable.
There is the samādhi of seeing dharmas as like reflections in water;
there is the samādhi of inexhaustible pure wisdom;
and there is the samādhi of the emptiness of persons, wherein all evils are absent and there is no perception of aspiration.
There is the samādhi of abiding in dhyāna that leads to nirvāṇa;
there is the samādhi which is like a vajra and free from defilement;
and there is the samādhi of infinite radiance.
There is the samādhi of having crossed over all afflictions and exhausted them;
there is the samādhi of the vast dharma of water;
there is the samādhi of the majestic great ship.
There is the samādhi of entering namelessness;
there is the samādhi of inexhaustible joyful intent;
there is the samādhi of dhāraṇī and non-forgetfulness.
There is the samādhi that causes all that is in darkness to become bright;
there is the samādhi that finds joy in whatever is joyful;
and there is the samādhi of compassionate conduct.
There is the samādhi of pure great compassion;
there is the samādhi of entering the impartial mind;
there is the samādhi of emerging from the impartial mind.
There is the samādhi known as "Already Liberated and Not Yet Liberated";
there is the samādhi of "The Source from Which Light Comes";
and there is the samādhi of "Awakening to That Which There Is Nothing One Does Not Awaken To."
There is the samādhi of liberation through wisdom and liberation through teaching;
there is the samādhi of manifesting golden lotus flowers;
and there is the samādhi of non-separation from impermanence.
There is the samādhi of venerable wisdom of non-arising;
there is the samādhi of valor that subdues all without exception;
there is the samādhi that opens up and reveals all buddha-fields.
There is the samādhi of purity in formlessness;
there is the samādhi of the nameless precious jewel;
there is the samādhi like the ocean that receives all things without exception.
"There is the Samādhi of Vast and Great Supernatural Power;
there is the Samādhi that reaches everywhere in the space of a finger-snap.
The Bodhisattva Dharmagatya said to Śāriputra:

"Because one dwells in the wisdom that is asked about, it is said to be 'inexhaustible. Hearing what is heard at the appropriate time according to one's wish, one does not become conceited; whatever one does is not false, and one always maintains respectful attention as instructed. By practicing wisdom and applying the mind without grasping, one does not lose propriety; the dharmas one practices are neither false nor confused."
The mind is like a precious jewel that eliminates all aging and illness; by taking the mind as the vessel for the Dharma, one finds joy in patience.
Whatever is contemplated is but thought, and whatever is delighted in is but the mental faculty of the Dharma; thus, wisdom never knows satiety.
In what is given, there is nothing to be begrudged; it is bestowed without partiality or favoritism.
Regarding what is asked, one observes with a mind fixed on the truth, rejoicing in the realization that nothing is attained.
When the mind is thus gladdened, the body becomes entirely light.
Their minds do not dwell on external paths; they desire only to hear the flavor of the Dharma and the Vīra-sūtra;
they desire only to hear upāyakauśalya (skillful means);
they desire only to hear the four types of equanimity of mind.
They desire only to hear the bottomless Dharma;
with a mind as it is, free from divergent thoughts, they desire to receive *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) through their intention;
they desire to hear the Dharma of non-arising and observe it without greed, desiring only to deliver others through compassion.
One who wishes to know the sound of impermanence;
one who wishes to know the meaning of stillness;
one who wishes to know emptiness within emptiness.
They have no desire to know about birth-and-death without perception or about giving;

they do not wish to hear anything at all, but only wish to hear music. Throughout the ten directions, they follow that music, acting with loyalty and faith to establish correctness, thereby subduing the faculties of all desires.
The Bodhisattva Dharmagadha rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When a bodhisattva has attained the Treasure Tathāgata Samādhi, acting spontaneously and having perfected all wisdom, they shall obtain the Three Jewels.”
What are the Three Jewels?

First, it is like a reflection in water: the reflection is neither within the water nor outside the water. When a bodhisattva sits in this space, his body is entirely present throughout the ten directions, yet his body is also not in the ten directions.

Second, while the Bodhisattva sits here, he manifests his divided bodies so that they all appear sitting before the Buddhas of the ten directions, yet his body does not actually sit before the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Third, it is like an echo in the mountains that responds to a call; the sound neither exists within nor without.

When a bodhisattva sits here and speaks of the affairs of all bodhisattvas in the ten directions from afar, none of those bodhisattvas in the ten directions come to him, nor does he go to them—thus it is!
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Dharmagupta:
"You have already attained the gate of dhāraṇī;
it is like holding a crossbow and laying out arrows—wherever you wish to shoot, there is nowhere they do not reach."
"A Bodhisattva takes a single wisdom and enters into ten thousand wisdoms, reaching everywhere—thus it is!
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Dharmagadha:

"When you see the Asuras wishing to raise their armies, in the mere snap of a finger their troops reach the twenty-eighth heaven without any interval; the Bodhisattva’s sequential entry from the ninth level downward when preaching the Dharma is just like this!"
The Tathāgata-Bodhisattva said to Śāriputra:

"As for purity, it is the subduing and elimination of desire; that mind which is free from desire is inexhaustible. Since various evil intentions can no longer disturb it, and because the mind guards against evil intentions, it is therefore inexhaustible.

As for the mind of anger, physical form, sensual desire, and pride—regarding all that is unsearcbable yet capable of being produced—the Bodhisattva constantly wishes to protect this mind. Knowing that it cannot be exhausted or removed, and seeing no defilements, one should know that this mind is inexhaustible."
When one protects those who are indolent, one should know that this intention is inexhaustible;
when one protects those who are deranged by protecting their own Dharma, one should know that this intention is boundless;
when one wishes to protect those lacking wisdom, one should know that this intention is limitless.
To bestow the Dharma upon all and liberate them through the Dharma—one should know that its intent is inexhaustible;
wishing to instruct all people so that they may all cultivate merit—one should know that its intent is beyond measure.
The Tathāgata said to Śāriputra:
“There are four dharmas of a bodhisattva. What are these four?”
First, the mental practice of dhāraṇī is inexhaustible.
Second, the practice of dhāraṇī is inexhaustible.
Third, the teaching of all people is inexhaustible.
"Fourth, because one never tires of study, the *dhāraṇī* is inexhaustible.
The Tathāgata and Bodhisattva spoke again to Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four things that are limitless."
First, the upper and middle liberations are inexhaustible.
Second, the path of the four horses is boundless.
Third, the king who acts according to his will is limitless.
"Fourth, the twelve links of dependent origination have no master and are inexhaustible.
It is in this way that they are 'inexhaustible.
Thus spoke the Tathāgata-Bodhisattva to Śāriputra.
"Furthermore, there are eight things that are inexhaustible. What are these eight?
First, the discourse on non-self is inexhaustible."
Second, the ultimate thought of non-action is inexhaustible.
Third, the discourse on the silent nirvana is inexhaustible.
Fourth, that which the bodhisattva delivers is inexhaustible.
Fifth, the flowing waters of the great ocean never weary and are inexhaustible.
Sixth, the absence of defilement from all evils is inexhaustible.
Seventh, the sounds of suffering and pain are inexhaustible.
Eighth, the perceptions of coming and going are inexhaustible.
These are the eight dharmas.
That which is to be delivered has no master and is inexhaustible.
The Tathāgata Bodhisattva said to Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are nine dharmas that are inexhaustible.
What are these nine dharmas?"
First, the Buddha-fields are inexhaustible.
Second, the places from which the bodhisattvas have come are inexhaustible.
Third, those who resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are inexhaustible.
Fourth, the incalculable loss of vows as one takes up the path of the Arhat or Pratyekabuddha;
fifth, the incalculable flight of Bodhisattvas from one Buddha-field to another throughout the ten directions.
Sixth, the six pāramitās are inexhaustible.
Seventh, the samādhis are inexhaustible.
Eighth, even that which transcends nirvāṇa is viewed as like an illusion and is thus inexhaustible.
"Ninth, the three realms are inexhaustible.
These are the nine dharmas that are inexhaustible.
Thus the Tathāgata spoke to Śāriputra.
“A bodhisattva possesses thirty-two jewels.
What are these thirty-two jewels?
First, their mind is not attached to sensual desires; this patience is inexhaustible, and it is thus a jewel.
Second, not giving rise to the notion of "self" or "non-self," and having nothing created, for this reason patience is inexhaustible; this is what constitutes a treasure.
Third, not dwelling upon any good or evil—this is patience that is inexhaustible, and this is what constitutes a treasure.
Fourth, to maintain a mind that is not constantly preoccupied with anything—this is the inexhaustible perfection of patience, and it is a treasure.
Fifth, to never harbor anger toward any person—this is the inexhaustible perfection of patience, and it is a treasure.
Sixth, not harboring thoughts of others' disorderly evils is the inexhaustible perfection of patience; this is itself a treasure.
Seventh, neither falsely harassing nor striking others is the inexhaustible perfection of patience; this is itself a treasure.
Eighth, not engaging in frivolous play within the great assembly; this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and it is a treasure.
Ninth, protecting one’s own person and protecting the persons of others; this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and it is a treasure.
Tenth, if one provides for those who are poor and destitute and thereafter harbors no expectation of anything in return, this is the inexhaustibility of patience; this is itself a treasure.
Eleventh, to protect oneself by not following evil associates and not following worldly assemblies—this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and it is a treasure.
Twelfth, to have no mind of craving or desire for one’s own body or the bodies of others—this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and it is a treasure.

Thirteenth: To not give rise to any conceptualizations and to have no thoughts of being a bodhisattva for even the duration of a finger-snap—this is the inexhaustible patience, and this is itself the jewel.
Fourteenth, protecting the physical marks adorned with merit; this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and it is a treasure.
Fifteenth, practicing goodness with faith without departing from samādhi; this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and it is a treasure.
Sixteenth, not speaking falsely with the mouth; this is the inexhaustible patience, which is itself a treasure.
Seventeenth, purity of mind; this is the inexhaustible patience, which is itself a treasure.

Eighteenth: Firmly abiding with a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), following them through life after life without abandoning them; not speaking of their faults or evils in other places—this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and this is itself a treasure.
Nineteenth: To reflect for oneself that if others have faults, one also has faults—this is the inexhaustible perfection of patience; this is itself a treasure.
Twentieth: when whatever one thinks of is immediately awakened to as being without deviation, this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
this is a treasure. Twenty-first: having a gentle heart and a peaceful mind, this is the inexhaustibility of patience; this is a treasure.
Twenty-second: To protect wicked people so that evil thoughts do not arise in their minds; this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and it is a treasure.
Twenty-third: To be born among the devas and to instruct the devas; this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and it is a treasure.

Twenty-fourth: being born in the heavens or the human world and being taught within the two paths so as not to undergo rebirth in the three evil realms—this is the inexhaustibility of patience; this is what constitutes a treasure.
Twenty-fifth: To be fully endowed with all the various marks of excellence—this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and this is itself a treasure.
Twenty-sixth: To attain a voice like the sound of Brahmā—this is the inexhaustibility of patience, and this is itself a treasure.
Twenty-seventh: To be liberated from lust, anger, and delusion—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
this is itself a treasure. Twenty-eighth: Not to dwell upon forms and names—this is the inexhaustibility of patience; this is itself a treasure.
Twenty-ninth: one does not cling to the merits performed, desiring only to give rise to all dharmas; this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
This is itself a treasure.
Thirty: To subdue all non-Buddhists is the inexhaustibility of patience; this is what constitutes a treasure. Thirty-one:
To have emerged from among the various lords is the inexhaustibility of patience; this is what constitutes a treasure.
"Thirty-second, to be fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas so that they are not injured or destroyed—this is the inexhaustibility of patience; this is what constitutes a treasure.
The Tathāgata and Bodhisattva said to Śāriputra:
"A bodhisattva has thirty-two matters that constitute treasures, just as they enter into them."
What are the thirty-two matters?
First, wishing to enter resonance, wishing to enter contemplation, yet having nothing to contemplate—this is itself the treasure.
Second, wishing to enter the mind, departing from the mind, and having no master over the mind—this is itself the treasure.
Third, when one desires to enter the body seeking liberation, yet finds that fundamentally there is no one to be liberated—this is the Jewel.
Fourth, when one does not enter the twelve links of dependent origination and remains without dwelling—this is the Jewel.
Fifth, wishing to enter cessation while remaining detached from non-cessation—this is the Jewel.
Sixth, wishing to enter impermanence while perceiving it as formless—this is the Jewel.
Seventh, wishing to enter the nameless while the master remains detached from the nameless—this is the jewel.
Eighth, wishing to enter quiescence without departing from arising—this is the jewel.
Ninth, wishing to enter the triple world yet not departing from the triple world—this is the jewel.
Tenth, wishing to enter into reception yet having nothing received—this is the jewel.
Eleventh, to wish to enter the future and the past, and likewise to emerge from the future and the past—this is the Jewel.
Twelfth, to wish to enter into merit while contemplating that it has no master from beginning to end—this is the Jewel.
Thirteenth, wishing to enter emptiness, yet remaining empty within emptiness—this is the Jewel.
Fourteenth, wishing to enter the signless, yet not giving rise to the signless—this is the Jewel.
Fifteenth: wishing to enter into vows, yet not giving rise to vows—this is the Jewel.
Sixteenth: wishing to enter into emptiness, yet remaining free from the conceptualization of emptiness—this is the Jewel.
Seventeenth: Desiring to enter samādhi without anything to which one is joined; why is this so?
Because dharmas have no duality—this is the jewel.
Eighteenth: Not having any aspiration for a place of rebirth by means of samādhi—this is the jewel.
Nineteenth, when samādhi does not serve as a realization of any phenomena, this is itself a treasure.
Twentieth, when one desires to enter the path of non-arising and there is one who attains deliverance, this is itself a treasure.
Twenty-first: wishing to enter the state of non-arising is itself a treasure.
Twenty-second: wishing to enter the state of immovability is itself a treasure.
Twenty-third: To desire to enter into all things as selfless, yet not to depart from selflessness—this is the Jewel.
Twenty-fourth: To desire to be fundamentally without mutual acquaintance with birth and death—this is the Jewel.
Twenty-fifth, when one desires to be without any initial cognition regarding samādhi, this is itself the jewel.
Twenty-sixth, when one desires to thoroughly know the characteristics through their mutual correspondence, this is itself the jewel.
Twenty-seventh: To desire to weary of and renounce the mind of desire—this is itself the treasure.
Twenty-eighth: To desire to enter into non-recollection and non-existence—this is itself the treasure.
Twenty-ninth: To wish to enter all the gates of *dhāraṇī* such that nothing is not encompassed—this is the jewel.
Thirtieth: To wish to enter into all committed evils, yet wishing not to commit evil—this is the jewel.
Thirty-first: wishing to enter *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and making the mind a vessel for the Dharma—this is the treasure.
Thirty-second: wishing to be in accord with all things without being distanced from them—this is the treasure.
The Buddha said to the Tathāgata:
"For example, if one wishes to enter a city, one must go through its gates; likewise, if one wishes to understand causes and conditions, there should be no contention.
If one wishes to understand contention, it is better not to engage in it oneself."

If one wishes to know how to avoid speech, it is better not to dwell in the midst of things; by remaining unmoving, do not allow desire to shift. One who has no expectations has no conceptualizations. Therefore, those who wish to remain equally free from peril should take their place in the correct position, for this is the ultimate state.
As for those who wish to possess nothing, they should guard their own house; those who can guard themselves do not engage in idle discourse.
One who is neither self-exalting nor self-deprecating is so because that person is already fully endowed [with virtue].
One who does not desire to be all-inclusive yet does not reproach others for what they lack, and who desires to employ others, will find that whatever is undertaken is never lost.
"Attaining the Way is likewise free from delusion; one who is free from delusion simply knows that all things are fundamentally non-existent.
Because one who knows fundamental non-existence has nothing to lose, the three periods of time are equal and without distinction."
That which neither increases nor decreases throughout the three periods of time does not dwell in form; having already not dwelt in form, it does not dwell in any phenomena.
When the eye sees form, it is merely the eye and the visual faculty that dwell upon this form;
when the ear hears sound, the consciousness of sound has no place of dwelling.
When the nose smells fragrance, the consciousness of fragrance has no place of abiding;
when the mouth perceives flavor, flavor likewise has no place of abiding;
when the body knows smoothness and texture, that consciousness also has no place of abiding.
The mind does not know consciousness, and consciousness does not know the mind;

there is no place of abiding. As in fundamental practice, there is no conceptualization; one practices wisdom according to the truth, and the truth is as it is for the self. There is no self and nothing belonging to a self. One does not perceive a self through the phenomena of consciousness; rather, the wisdom that perceives only the designation of "non-self" does not know any existing things, nor does it know wisdom itself.
Desire does not know its own accumulation; accumulation does not know wisdom; wisdom does not know the body; and the body does not know wisdom.
That the Bodhisattva’s mind does not depart from that mind—is this not so?
The Bodhisattva Dharmagadha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O God among Gods!
The Way does not unite with conceptualization; is there, then, anything that unites?”
The Buddha said to the bodhisattva:
"One does not take all dharmas as proof, but takes only sounds as the dharma.

It is like a person blowing a long flute; the sound is mournful yet delightful and blends with the song, such that one knows the breath of the song and the breath of the flute have combined to produce a single sound."
The various samādhis of the bodhisattvas are also like this: all dharmas are without arising or destruction, and they are likewise free from cessation;
the various emanations are also like this, the various thoughts are also like this, and the various awakenings are also like this!
All births are nameless and free from namelessness;
all thoughts are nameless and free from namelessness;
all transformations are nameless and free from namelessness.
One awakens to the absence of all names and is detached from namelessness.
There is no place where I do not contemplate this; it is simply that the thought of non-action constitutes detachment.

When one has already attained the state of non-acting action, one has already formed the thought of action; yet, with the cessation of thought and volition, there is total non-attachment, for all phenomena are devoid of desire and are thus entirely so.
The Tathāgata adjusted his robes and addressed the Perfectly Enlightened One, saying:
"All dharmas are unarisen; I now wish to ask the Tathāgata about what the Bodhisattva Dharmagatya asked previously:
'How shall we resolve our great doubts and each return to our original place?'"
The Buddha said to the Tathāgata:
"If all dharmas arise, they have no place;
if they are manifested, they have no place."
"All dharmas are either the station of awakening or not the station of awakening;
all dharmas are either the station of mindfulness or not the station of mindfulness.
Thus the Bodhisattva addressed the Tathāgata, the God among Gods, saying:
"In the place of birth-and-birth, is there birth?
In the place of transformation-and-transformation, is there transformation?
In the place of non-thought, is there thought?"
"In a state without perception, is there perception or not?
The Tathāgata replied:
"Birth after birth, and further birth, and the birth of nirvāṇa—this is 'conjunction. Yet the intention of the Tathāgata is not conjunction."
If birth after birth gives rise again to non-arising nirvāṇa, this is not in accord; the intention of the Tathāgata is what is in accord.
If transformation after transformation gives rise again to transformative nirvāṇa, this is considered in accord; the intention of the Tathāgata is not in accord.
If transformation after transformation gives rise again to non-transformative nirvāṇa, this is considered not in accord; the intention of the Tathāgata is what is in accord.
To be mindful of Nirvāṇa in every thought after thought is "conformity," yet it is not conformity with the intention of the Tathāgata;
to be mindless of Nirvāṇa in every thought after thought is "non-conformity," yet it is conformity with the intention of the Tathāgata;
to be awakened to Nirvāṇa in every awakening after awakening is "conformity," yet it is not conformity with the intention of the Tathāgata.
"To awaken, to awaken again, and to awaken to non-awakening—that is Nirvana. Awakening is non-conjunction; the intention of the Tathāgata is conjunction.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva spoke in verse:
"The Dharma has no arising; Conjunction is but a single moment!"
Life after life does not arise again; nirvāṇa is entirely like this.
That which is transformed is originally non-existent; in transformation upon transformation, there is no one who is liberated.
Transformation is equal to nirvāṇa; it is quiescent and has no location.
Thought is fundamentally without consciousness; the arising of thought is due to emptiness alone!
Nirvāṇa is equal to thought, and that which is contemplated is truly thus.
Awareness and awareness are equal and even; that which is realized reaches nowhere.
That which is realized has no permanence; therefore, it is the Tathāgata.
The place of transformation has no location, and that which is realized reaches nowhere.
If transformation has no locus, all dharmas are likewise so.
The place of birth has neither origin nor existence; non-arising is its true locus.
The place of transformation is nameless; all things are thus samādhi.
In the foundations of mindfulness, mindfulness both exists and does not exist; from emptiness one arrives at this state.
It is not that there is originally nothing to be realized; such is the nature of his wisdom.
Awakening does not proceed by way of succession, nor does awakening depart from its own place.
Practice follows awakening to see the truth; apart from awakening, there is no liberation.
The dharmas that arise are unceasing; wherever they abide, it is always thus.
Among the suns and moons of the three thousandfold world system, there is no light superior to this.
These dharmas are beyond conceptual thought, yet they can be realized by those who practice.
He gives rise to no defilement regarding desire; he is neither in emptiness nor in perception.
The Tathāgata’s mind is ever pure, yet he does not dwell in the names of dharmas.
That which is liberated is neither permanent nor abiding; all things remain as they were in their original state.
Flowers and incense come forth spontaneously, yet they have no place of origin;
