"All dharmas have already ceased," [the Buddha said].
The king questioned the Buddha about this matter with great joy; for a hundred days, day and night, he took delight solely in this samādhi.
The king paid homage to the Buddha and returned to his seat, whereupon he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata, the Bodhisattvas, and the venerable elders who are Bodhisattvas from distant lands have all come from afar; I fear that if they meet with the Buddha now, they will simply depart.
I now wish to request that Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Bodhisattvas, and the others come to my home for a meal; may the Tathāgata grant me this wish!”
The Buddha remained silent and gave no reply, which was taken as his acceptance.

The king prostrated before the Buddha and returned to his palace, where he immediately commanded his ministers to quickly have the kingdom adorned. Along both sides of the road, fragrant flowers and famous blossoms were arranged;
along both sides of the road, canopies of flowers were formed, and the royal palace was swept clean.
All the finest flowers and incenses in the world were fashioned into a hundred kinds of seats, all made of lapis lazuli, gold, and silver;
the palace was thoroughly swept and cleansed, and all the queens and court ladies observed the fast and precepts.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgatas, and the others all proceeded to the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
Upon entering the city, before they had reached the palace gates, the king came out to welcome the bodhisattvas!
At that time, there were sixty billion beings, including the Bodhisattvas Tathāgata and Mañjuśrī.
The Tathāgata yielded precedence, allowing them to enter the palace first; the various venerable Bodhisattvas did not enter the palace ahead of him.
The Tathāgata said,
"Venerable Bodhisattvas, for what reason do you not enter the palace first?
Venerable Bodhisattvas ought to enter first."
The Tathāgata said:
"I shall not enter the palace first; the venerable bodhisattvas should enter.
The bodhisattvas said:
"What constitutes being venerable?
To have no locus within wisdom is itself venerable;
to have no form within the mind is therefore venerable."
He is venerable because he does not conceptualize within mindfulness;
he is venerable because he bestows nothing upon phenomena;
he is venerable because his actions do not depart from the Path.
He is venerable because he has already severed the wheel of Dharma;
he is venerable because he is without mindfulness of dharmas and without conceptualization of them;
he is venerable because there is no increase or decrease regarding dharmas.
He is venerable because his skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) are exceedingly vast;
he is venerable because he possesses no conceptual cognition regarding omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
he is venerable because he has donned the armor of the Dharma.
"In samādhi there is neither excess nor deficiency; therefore, he is venerable.
One who is thus is a Tathāgata, and for this reason should enter the palace first.
Thus spoke the Tathāgata to the Bodhisattva.
"Therefore, by what standard is one venerable? Is it because of age that one is venerable?
The bodhisattvas replied:

"Now, although our age may be greater than that of the Venerable One, we are like a withered, dead tree ten thousand years old; its roots have long since perished, and it no longer possesses flowers or fruit capable of providing shade or shelter for the world."

Although the Tathāgata is now young in years, his entry into wisdom is exceedingly profound; he is like a jewel tree among people, from which those who obtain its flowers and fruits all attain deliverance.
"The deceased shall enter the palace first.
The Tathāgata entered first, and the various honored devas followed with ten thousand kinds of music, playing as they went.
Mañjuśrī and the Tathāgata each took their seats.

The King had his consort prepare golden vessels for the food of the various bodhisattvas, all of which contained the eight kinds of flavors; within the palace, ten thousand varieties of blended incense were burned.
When the meal was finished, the King addressed Mañjuśrī and the Tathāgata, saying:
"I now wish to behold the great assembly of the Buddhas of the ten directions; by what means may this be accomplished?"
The Tathāgata said:
"Those who wish to see the assemblies of the Buddhas of the ten directions and wish to see all those of manifold wisdom need only practice nine dharmas.
What are these nine?"
First, one should regard the Buddhas of the ten directions as no different from this [Buddha].
Second, one should regard my path as having no further path to be traversed.
Third, one should contemplate that among all people, there is none who has attained liberation.
Fourth, one should regard food and drink as something seen through transformation.
Fifth, one should know that the five aggregates possess neither consciousness nor perception.
Sixth, one should know that the six sense organs are merely like illusions when observed!
Seventh, one should know that contemplation is merely a perverted view.
Eighth, one should practice great giving within the Dharma.
Ninth, one should know that what is given is not truly given.
When the king heard that the Tathāgata had explained it thus, he rejoiced and withdrew to sit down.
At that time, the Buddha smiled and said:
"How wonderful, how wonderful!"
The Tathāgata spoke these verses for him:
"One should always manifest this merit, so that wherever one is born, one may always encounter the Honored One.
From receiving great wisdom, one shall forever eliminate the root of craving and desire."
Neither greedy nor envious, no evil thoughts arise again;
having followed countless Buddhas, they have heard this samādhi.
Thus, throughout the three thousand worlds, they constantly practice this honored samādhi.
Not toward any person, nor toward all precious jewels;
the Dharma does not arise from the five aggregates, nor is it apart from this state.
Liberation is attained through contemplation; all things are thus!
Through contemplation, one attains joy; the resolve thus generated is without arising.
Since his state is already such as this, he is the God among Gods.
Even if he were within the triple world, he would neither be born nor die.
Nirvāṇa and nirvṛti—none of these exist! The mind should not harbor wrong thoughts, nor should one engage in unrighteous conduct;
even while within the three realms, one must maintain the mind so that it does not arise [with such thoughts].
Sounds have echoes that respond, Inner and outer are entirely in accord;
Without arising, all is utterly tranquil— All phenomena are likewise so!
The three thousand buddha-fields, Their names are all thus!
Neither hearing nor seeing exists; it is not a dharma that can be deliberated upon.
Samādhi is beyond calculation; having already counted, one maintains it as manifold.
The wise who understand these words attain the Buddha’s ocean of impermanence.
The Dharma is entirely pure, vast and without peer;
it constantly acts as boundless water, carrying all while encompassing the three thousandfold world.
One’s aspiration for the *dhāraṇī* gives rise to wisdom that has no predecessor.
Since the Dharma is thus, all should practice it accordingly.
When I reflect upon the time I sought my aspiration, throughout many kalpas since then,
my resolve has always been to leave the household life, seeking nothing at all within the realm of desire.
Constantly relying on spiritual friends, one establishes and abides in the True Dharma;
at that time, within the great assembly, one hears of this honored samādhi.
With a mind of great joy, one immediately dwells in the midst of space.
Rising one hundred and forty *zhang* above the ground, he stood with palms joined beside the Buddha.
Now these seated bodhisattvas receive their individual predictions in the same way!
Their minds are filled with increasing joy as they hear of all the samādhis.
Then, from a single buddha-field, they fly before all the Buddhas;
without moving or shaking, they cause all the fields to tremble.
Fragrant flowers arrive spontaneously, and turbulent winds arise naturally.
A hundred kinds of musical instruments were all present within the seats.
The Dragon King was greatly delighted and immediately rained down ten thousand varieties of incense;
these transformed into numerous small ponds, reaching as far as the three thousandfold world system.
The Tathāgata addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

"Now these natural flowers and fragrances have come from three thousand world-systems to this assembly, and all the musical instruments are fully provided; is this the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, the supernormal power of the Tathāgata?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Tathāgata, saying:

"If you wish to know the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and that of the various bodhisattvas, it cannot be seen or known. This is the joy in which those who delight abide—the joy that is nameless. Wherever there is the Dharma, there is the nameless state; whether it be suffering or joy, this is the place of joy."
"All things are merely like transformations; this is their joy.
The Dharma is non-dual; this is its joy.
To desire to deliver all arhats and pratyekabuddhas; this is its joy."
To desire that all those seen in the five realms of existence may attain Buddhahood—this is their joy.
That there is no birth in all those who are delivered—this is their joy.
That all things are without location and without arising—this is their joy.
To be without the burden of mental affliction within samādhi is its joy.
To be nameless in all places is its joy.
That all that exists is like a magical illusion is its joy.
That which is not a locus of sound and has no place of arising—this is its bliss.
That which is bestowed by the Dharma yet involves no bestowing and nothing that exists—this is its bliss.
That within the three thousandfold world-system there is no place of permanence—this is its bliss.
To cause all people to attain faith while realizing there is nothing to be attained—this is their joy.
That in the three periods of future, past, and present, everything is utterly inexhaustible—this is their joy.
To cause one to return to the fundamental non-perception is its joy.
To see the Wheel of Dharma as being without anything seen is its joy.
That all three thousandfold world systems are equal is its joy.
The treasuries of the Dharma within the three thousandfold worlds of the ten directions—this is their joy.
That all lands in the ten directions exist as mere names—this is their joy.
The union of form and desire—this is their joy.
That names have no master is its bliss.
That all is boundless and utterly quiescent is its bliss.
That all light and darkness are unified is its bliss.
That all one's actions do not lose their precepts is its joy.
That all one's thoughts do not depart from samādhi is its joy.
That the perfection of the reality of empty space is its joy.
That all wisdom and awakening have no location is their bliss.
That all things are acceptable is their bliss.
That there is ultimately no recipient of anything is their bliss.
To have no equal within the three realms—this is its joy.
To crave the Dharma without sparing one's life—this is its joy.
When all wisdoms unite and become even more luminous—this is its joy.
To have no inverted views regarding all that exists is its joy.
To practice giving without expectation is its joy.
To possess a boundless mind as a great captain of the ship is its joy.
To be liberated from the boundless gardens is its joy;
for the mind to be tranquil is its joy;
to have no fixed abode is its joy.
That no one attains any of the gates of samādhi is their joy.
That there is neither listening nor hearing is their joy.
That all thoughts are not the right path is their joy.
That all people are infinite is their joy.
That all those who are delivered are like illusions is their joy.
That the initial resolve is endowed with samādhi is their joy.
That all Bodhisattvas have no place from which they come is their joy.
That all Bodhisattvas travel throughout the ten directions by means of the mind is their joy.
That there is no path that is blue, yellow, white, or black is their joy.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said to the Tathāgata:
"If you wish to know the majestic spiritual power and the aspirations of the Buddhas and all bodhisattvas, their various aspirations are just like this!"
Mañjuśrī answered the Tathāgata regarding the bodhisattva’s inquiry on the five delights, and the Tathāgata then spoke these verses:
“O Mañjuśrī, your mind Is a supreme wisdom with no predecessor;
The merit of your giving eclipses the three thousandfold world, And there is none whose wisdom is not honored by you.”
The deeds performed through majestic spiritual power completely eliminate [suffering] within the three thousandfold world system;
having no desire for any worldly pleasures, he gives only so that they may not be taken away.
To delight in the Dharma is the greatest thing; among those to be transformed, there are none who cannot be saved.
The gift of the Dharma is given with joy; if it is empty, there is no evil.
The Dharma is accompanied by joy; there is no treasure greater than this.
That which is cherished has no owner; if it is empty, it has no fixed location.
Deeply penetrating all that is subtle and wondrous, he brings understanding to all people;
he enables them to attain the Great Dharma and sever the roots of diligent suffering.
All people in the world possess minds that do not understand.
Taking the Dharma as the basis for awakening, one uses wisdom to save all beings.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
“To be detached from emptiness yet not devoid of perception—this is perception that is not empty;”
To not give rise to [conceptions] regarding phenomena is itself their arising.
One should always maintain a gentle mind, pure and devoid of anything possessed;
though form and desire may coincide, there is no one who enters into them.
That which is spoken of as formless does not exist apart from form;
because phenomena are like dreams, that which is desired is bottomless.
This is quiescence and detachment from quiescence; there is no detachment, for nothing is created.
All phenomena have no master; they are like transformations.
There is nothing at all to be received, and no phenomenon to be abandoned;
all inverted views are likewise thus.
It is not form, yet it is apart from form; it is that which is separated from form.
Its nature is like form, and its locus is likewise!
It is not sound, yet it is an echo; there is neither hearing nor seeing.
Neither hearing nor observing—such is the nature of all things!
In ritual there is no name, yet one claims it to be right;
in the Dharma there is no such calculation, for that which is delivered is thus!
In illusion there is no seeing; what is seen is free from seeing.
Free from attachment to desire, it is not a matter for debate.
In desire there is no defilement; one neither clings nor departs.
"Seeing thus with such clarity, there is no one who sees.
Knowing the Buddha’s smile, the Bodhisattva spoke these verses within the palace:
"Doubt is fundamentally unresolvable; / One says that dharmas are spontaneous (svabhāva)."
Fundamentally there is no permanence; neither doubt nor wisdom exists therein.
To be without toil regarding perceptions and without suffering in mindfulness—this is what is meant by "raising names and abiding in words"; it is not for those who seek the Dharma.
Fundamentally it is not so; there is no returning and no retreating.
That which is "nothing" is itself beyond being "nothing.
In arising there is no cessation—this is itself cessation.
To have no conceptualization regarding meaning is not extinction;
to have no arising regarding phenomena is likewise not the extinction of characteristics. Why is this so?
All phenomena are empty.
Furthermore, one does not seek to say, "I am detached from nirvāṇa. Why is this so?
Because both the root and the branches are pure,
one does not exhaust the ten directions; taking this up as a witness,
to say "this is me" is itself the witness.
One should not dwell on distant thoughts, but rather contemplate the ten directions;
the true Dharma is not vexing, for this reception is nameless.
The Dharma is not an object of recollection, yet it is that which should be returned to.
Acting in this manner, one does not perceive the Honored Dharma.
One must understand through wisdom and remain unafraid of the profound;
wandering aimlessly leads nowhere—this may be called the gateway to wisdom.
The Tathāgata asked Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:
“Among those gathered today who have newly resolved their minds, I wish to enable them to attain the infinite Dharma; by what means may this be accomplished?”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
"By being non-active within mindfulness, one may attain the infinite Dharma.
The Tathāgata asked again:
“What is meant by ‘mindfulness that there is no agent’?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Tathāgata:
“One should establish the nine dharmas of the Jewel.”
What are the nine treasures of the Dharma?
First, the mind has no abiding place; this is itself a treasure.
Second, observing that dharmas have no master; this is itself a treasure.
Third, not perceiving the existence of either the future or the past—this is itself the jewel.
Fourth, that within all phenomena there is no creator—this is itself the jewel.
Fifth, to give only the sound of the Dharma as a gift—this is a jewel.
Sixth, to see the suffering within the five realms of existence and yet have one’s mind not waver therein—this is a jewel.
Seventh, that which is realized is not distant from *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means); this is itself a treasure.
Eighth, to see all phenomena directly and not abide in duality; this is itself a treasure.
"Ninth, even reaching nirvana is like a transformation; this is the Jewel.
The Tathāgata said to Śāriputra, "These are the nine Dharma Jewels."
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva spoke in verse:
"There is nothing to laugh at; that which is done is called impermanent.
If one is empty and free from defilement, there is nothing for which the Buddha would not smile."
Laughing at emptiness is not separate from the phenomenal; as it is originally so, there is nothing to laugh at.
Once one abides in the names of all dharmas, everything is like laughter.
Both the fundamental and the derivative are spontaneous; there is no coming or going.
One who laughs has a response; one who does not respond does not laugh.
All phenomena (dharmas) are one; through laughing, there is duality.
Within duality there are no names; therefore, he is the Honored One.
That which is laughed at has nothing to be approved; it is solely for the sake of bestowing the gift of all dharmas.
That which is moved has nothing that moves; therefore, he is the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Mañjuśrī replied to the Tathāgata in verse:
“The one who laughs has no retribution; all things have no master.
That laugh does not depart from the source; therefore, he is the God among Gods.
The one who laughs has no destination; it is merely for the sake of those with inverted views!”
All phenomena are utterly tranquil; in this tranquility, there is fundamentally nothing that exists.
The one who smiles does not depart from transformation, yet through transformation he bestows the Great Gift.
Within transformation there is no name to be raised; therefore, this is the Dharma.
In the Dharma there is no such thing as "is," yet he practices giving for the sake of those not yet liberated;
though already liberated, he does not regard himself as liberated—such is the Buddha.
Therefore, within this great assembly, he deliberates upon those who have crossed over and those who have not.
Bestowing gifts upon the Dharma is beyond compare;
it is tranquil and detached from tranquility, free from detachment and non-creation.
All phenomena have no master; their destination is like a magical transformation.
Śāriputra again asked the Tathāgata:
"If one wishes to cause those in the ten directions who have resolved their minds to practice the *dhāraṇī*, what dharma should they practice?
"They should practice the thirty-two treasures of the Dharma."
“What are the thirty-two treasures of the Dharma?
Mañjuśrī replied: “The first treasure of the Dharma is the desire to deliver all those throughout the ten directions who have not yet resolved their minds, treating them as if they were emanations.”
The second Jewel of the Dharma is to cause all who have not yet resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to abide in the True Dharma.
The third Jewel of the Dharma is to desire that the suns and moons of the trichiliocosm be seen as equal in all respects.

The four treasures of the Dharma are: if one abides in the mind, they cause all to distance themselves from manifold desires; through the gateway of wisdom, remaining unmoving and unshakable, one reaches Nirvāṇa.
The five treasures of the Dharma are: when people speak of the existence of heaven or the non-existence of heaven, one’s resolve remains unmoved and returns [to its source].
The sixth jewel of the Dharma is that the mind remains unmoved and returns [to its source].
The seventh jewel of the Dharma is that all who are without coming or receiving birth view the future and the past as being non-dual.
The eighth jewel of the Dharma is to contemplate all samādhis and dhyānas as tranquil and devoid of location.
The ninth jewel of the Dharma is that all those who are delivered have no master; everything is led from emptiness back to emptiness.
Regarding the tenth treasure of the Dharma: I have received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas of the three thousandfold world-systems of suns and moons.

Regarding the eleventh treasure of the Dharma: among the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three thousandfold world-systems of suns and moons, all who venture to come and listen to this sutra shall receive the prediction of Buddhahood; those who likewise abide in the midst of space shall do so as well.

Regarding the twelve treasures of the Dharma: in the buddha-fields of all Buddhas, flowers, incense, and natural silk canopies arrive of their own accord; yet those that arrive do not bring joy, and those that do not arrive are not sought after.
The thirteenth jewel of the Dharma is that it causes all who dare to resolve their minds to abide in the Dharma according to its proper place.
The fourteenth jewel of the Dharma is that there is neither increase nor decrease regarding the future or the past.
Why is this? Because one knows that, from the beginning, there are no two [natures].

As for the fifteen jewels of the Dharma, they all desire to cause the crawling and flying creatures of the ten directions to uphold the Buddha’s sutras and precepts so that they remain unhurt and unimpaired.
The sixteenth jewel of the Dharma is to be free from wrong thoughts; when the mind turns toward the ten directions, it returns to its source and thus proceeds toward the gate of wisdom.
The seventeenth jewel of the Dharma is to constantly practice patience.
The eighteenth treasure of the Dharma is that from one contemplation to another there is no one who crosses over.
The nineteenth treasure of the Dharma is that what abides fundamentally has no place of permanent residence; thus it has no place of permanent residence.

The twenty-first jewel of the Dharma: that which is to be delivered has no master; it is called "emptiness. To bestow upon the multitude what they desire within the impermanent realm of desire—for this reason, it is the Path.

The twenty-second jewel of the Dharma: to bestow wisdom as a gift is to give without any sense of self-aggrandizement; regarding desires, there is nothing to be grasped, for it is solely for the sake of liberation.

The twenty-second jewel of the Dharma is called the Great Dharma because what is taught does not deviate from giving in accordance with causes, and thus those who attain it are liberated and never again subject to rebirth.
The twenty-third jewel of the Dharma is that one constantly flies to the presence of a single Buddha across countless Buddha-fields.
The twenty-fourth treasure of the Dharma is that throughout the lands of the ten directions, there is no one who can escape [the nature of reality].
The twenty-fifth treasure of the Dharma is that purity and delusion are unified in accordance with the fundamental purity, without distinction.
The twenty-sixth jewel of the Dharma is that, by abiding within the three thousandfold world-system and acting as a bridge, one’s progress in study is like seeing light in the darkness.
The twenty-seventh jewel of the Dharma is that, constantly acting as a great master mariner upon the boundless waters, those whom one ferries across are without limit.
The twenty-eighth jewel of the Dharma is that which constantly acts as a boundless canopy, closing off the defilements of the three thousandfold world system.
The twenty-ninth jewel of the Dharma is that which constantly acts as infinite wisdom, never departing from the ten directions.

Regarding the thirty treasures of the Dharma: they constantly exercise great compassion throughout the ten directions, delivering all who have not yet been delivered and liberating all who have not yet been liberated; therefore, he who is without characters is called the God among Gods.

Regarding the thirty-first treasure of the Dharma: practicing equanimity without peer, toward both the non-existent and toward persons, he is designated as the Unsurpassed Honored One; because his resolve is impartial, he is therefore called a Buddha.

Regarding the thirty-two treasures of the Dharma: the Tathāgata, as the Honored One, has taught that these do not depart from the Dharma; they are heard throughout the three thousandfold world-systems, where space itself acts as the sovereign of spontaneity, and thus they are established within flowers and incense.
Such are the thirty-two dharma-jewels of the Bodhisattva!
"The great transformation throughout the ten directions—everything is called impermanent;
the true Dharma is not a burden to bear—it is thus taught that one delivers the ten directions."
Possessing perception yet not departing from perception, all treasures are empty;
whether flowers or leaves, their colors cannot be withstood.
Amidst the sphere of all desires, he stands as the King of the Mind.
The Most Honored One among all jewels, Known as the God among Gods,
Therefore, within this great assembly, Discusses the deliverance of those who have no escape;
Since his essence is fundamentally without permanence, He is titled the Honored One of the Ten Directions.
All things are seen as inverted; the worldly means of pleasure are like transformations.
If one can perceive them thus, one may be liberated from the ten directions.
Within the impermanent space of emptiness, the Buddha-treasury is entirely contained.
Already liberated, there is nothing further to be liberated; therefore, he teaches throughout the ten directions.
All the Buddha-fields of the ten directions are joined together as a single land;
naturally, great assemblies fill every part of the ten directions.
The Buddha is the Awakened One of all; his smile never leaves his countenance, nor does he ever depart from his golden hue.
Having already shown the way to those not yet liberated, he acts as the path for the ten directions; his mind never departs from the Dharma King.
In giving, there is nothing given; one offers flowers as alms throughout the ten directions.
Golden great lotus flowers fill the entirety of every buddha-field;
yet though they give rise to thoughts and perform deeds, they do not abide among the various heavens.
The mind of Mañjuśrī is vast and peerless;
it is like one who has first received a prophecy, dwelling in the midst of space.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom-mind is supreme; its radiance pervades the entire palace.
All those celestial beings of pleasing mind have fully attained the gateway to the Dharma.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions cause all lands to tremble;
now these celestial beings gathered in this assembly have been able to hear this honored sutra.
Piercingly seeing all things, he then arrives at the Palace of Delight;
it transforms into a jeweled lattice seat, filled with myriad kinds of celestial flowers and fragrances.
There he listens to and receives various samādhis, sitting and observing the great assembly.
All those who have come with past merits, having resolved their minds to make offerings to the Honored One—
those on the Path do not see them fully, for all things are thus;
the various liberations are beyond numbering, and the three realms are inexhaustible.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī asked the Tathāgata Bodhisattva:
"All sounds are like transformations; that which is produced regarding phenomena is without conceptualization and is also inexhaustible, thus it possesses spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
By what means should one be liberated from this?"
The Tathāgata Bodhisattva spoke to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:
“Furthermore, there are nine dharmaratnas.
What are these nine dharmaratnas?”
The first Jewel of Dharma is that which is spontaneously non-existent and like an illusion.
The second Jewel of Dharma is that all phenomena are non-existent and like an illusion.
The third Jewel of Dharma is that the future is non-existent and like an illusion.
The fourth jewel of the Dharma is that all existing things are worldly, direct locations, and are like magical transformations.
The fifth jewel of the Dharma is that one contemplates past locations as being like magical transformations as well.
The sixth jewel of the Dharma is that one perceives all phenomena as being merely like illusions, having no fixed location and being like transformations.
The seventh jewel of the Dharma is that even that which has no location is likewise like a transformation.
The eighth jewel of the Dharma is that attaining the Way is without a place of liberation, and it is also like a transformation.
The ninth jewel of the Dharma is that attaining nirvana is fundamentally without a place of abiding, and it is also like a transformation.
Mañjuśrī asked again: “Tathāgata!
That which transcends nirvāṇa is entirely spontaneous; who is the basis for this transformation?”
Who is the master of transformation?
Is that which is transformed fundamentally non-existent?
Or is it non-existent at the place where the transformation arises?
“Is there no path and no place?
The Tathāgata and Bodhisattva said to Mañjuśrī:
“Furthermore, there are nine dharmas:”
First, transformation occurs where there is no place for transformation; since the non-place is not a path, this is itself transformation.
Second, the non-place is without conceptualization; this is itself transformation.
Third, regarding the Three Jewels, the non-place is transformed into a locus; this is itself transformation.
Regarding the fourth treasure of Dharma: that which is not a permanent name and is inexhaustible is itself an emanation.
Regarding the fifth treasure of Dharma: that there is no place for the locus of emanation is itself an emanation.
The sixth jewel of the Dharma is that there is no conceptualization regarding the Path; this is transformation.
The seventh jewel of the Dharma is that there is no arising within arising; this is transformation.
The eighth jewel of the Dharma is that there is no locus of desire within all desires; this is transformation.
"The Ninefold Jewel of the Dharma consists in that there is no one to be saved and nothing to be saved;
this is transformation. Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva spoke in verse to answer the Tathāgata:
"In the ten directions there is no one who transforms, And transformation upon transformation has no form."
All treasures are impermanent; therefore, they are produced through transformation.
The Way is not attained through transformation, nor does it depart from its place;
that which is described as having an impermanent form naturally abides in its place.
All phenomena arise from transformation; fundamentally they are detached and non-existent.
Their origin is born of transformation; therefore, he is the Honored One among men.
Desire arises from transformation; in the fundamental nature of phenomena, it does not exist.
Manifesting and dwelling within the five realms, yet no one perceives the master of these manifestations;
death, birth, and the five realms are not connected to this manifestation;
because worldly craving is not severed, the Truly Awakened One appears!
The Tathāgata and the Lord of Emanations, the supreme and infinite Honored One of the ten directions;
he sustains emanations and bestows great gifts upon the world, yet none in the world know him.
The Wheel of Dharma turns without form, and within the world there is no one who turns it.
Bound to form and possessing thought, the profound Dharma has no turner.
One’s perception of form transforms the ten directions; there is none who does not receive the Dharma.
As for the great wisdom bestowed, there is none in the world who hears it.
All desires and arhats, non-returners and these jewels—therefore, within this great assembly, he is the unsurpassed jewel who brings liberation.
His wisdom is inexhaustible; his radiance is supreme and beyond compare.
Acting as a bridge for the ten directions, what they teach is without duality.
May all the buddha-fields of the ten directions be made entirely equal;
nor shall those people be allowed to give rise to thoughts of divergent minds.
The gardens of all dharmas in the ten directions, where all abide free from defilement;
they do not arise from the world, and regarding these dharmas, none can take them away.
In wisdom there is no liberation, for one sees neither those who come nor those who go.
In stillness one perceives stillness again; within clarity one perceives clarity once more.
The Dharma is not attained through wisdom; it is spontaneously such that it has no origin or basis.
Wisdom and the darkness of ignorance are both equally merged, such that there is ultimately no one who recognizes them.
Ignorance and wisdom do not coexist; that wisdom illuminates the multitude of darknesses.
What is bestowed is solely for the sake of the Dharma, like flowers upon a high mountain.
All evils cannot be exhausted, nor can sensual desires be brought to an end.
Nirvāṇa and saṃsāra—everything is thus.
The wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions is without knowing and without perceiving;
because they perceive pure phenomena, it is said that such things do not exist in the world.
The Bodhisattva Dharmagadha again asked the Tathāgata, the Bodhisattva:
"In the transformation that is without arising or departure, who becomes the master?

Nirvāṇa is neither born nor extinguished, and it does not distance one from the five realms of existence; yet it causes those who have first resolved their minds to turn and abide in the Wheel of Dharma, free from all defilements, so that [all phenomena] may never arise again—who is it that delivers them?"
The Tathāgata said:
“Dharmagupta’s question seeks to sever the roots of birth and death throughout the ten directions; such is the way one should practice the Ninefold Dharma-Jewel.”
What are the nine Dharma-jewels?
First, that which is without a master is itself a jewel.
Second, the Dharma-jewel is that wherein Nirvana and birth-and-death have never had mutual knowledge from the very beginning; this is itself a jewel.
The threefold Dharma Jewel: that which arises in birth and death yet remains unextinguished in cessation—this is the Jewel.
The fourfold Dharma Jewel: that which reaches upward to the thirty-six heavenly beings so as not to return to the place of birth in birth and death—this is the Jewel.
Regarding the five dharma-jewels: when the intention has arisen or has not yet arisen, it abides as it is; this is the jewel. Regarding the six dharma-jewels:
observing the three-thousandfold world-system of Buddha-fields, one realizes there is no one to be delivered; this is the jewel.
The seventh jewel of the Dharma is that wherein mindfulness has no place of arising; this is itself the jewel.
The eighth jewel of the Dharma is to cause all three thousandfold Buddha-fields to enter nirvāṇa without the mind feeling joy, and not entering nirvāṇa without the mind feeling anger. Why is this so?
Because all dharmas have no fixed location, this is itself the Jewel.
As for the ninefold Dharma-Jewel: according to their vows, those who seek arhatship—I cause all such as have resolved to seek it to never again turn back from that vow; this is itself the Jewel.
To not give rise to any births and to have no returning vows—this is precisely the Dharma Jewel of the Bodhisattva.
The Tathāgata answered the Bodhisattva Dharmagatya, speaking in verse:
“In that which is acceptable, there is nothing to be accepted; In desire, there is no desiring.”
That which is to be delivered has no seer; the Wheel of Dharma has no fixed abode.
The wise have nothing to proclaim; because they deliver through causes, there is no one who goes.
Thus one perceives the Great Right Dharma, the most supreme thing in the world.
The Way has no constant name, and thus it is the treasure of the ten directions;
having attained non-attainment, there is no Way within birth and death.
The four horses can never be exhausted, and the agreeable mind knows no satiety.
Those who delight entirely in the world neither abandon it nor attain the Way.
Fearing birth, there is no liberation; not fearing it, there is no one liberated.
When the cycle of birth and death is given a name, it is established as the five destinies.
That which has a response but no answer may be called this Dharma;
the Dharma is fundamentally non-dual, and all truths have already been awakened to.
It is boundless and without limit, infinite and incalculable.
The ultimate limit is like a shadow or an echo; there is no one who comes or goes.
In arising, there is nothing that arises; phenomena are devoid of all desires.
Birth and death have no fundamental location; such is the transformation of birth and death.
In purity there is no purity; in defilement there is no defilement.
For the sake of all people in the ten directions, they sever the bonds of the five realms of existence.
Their pure minds are like water, entirely free from blemish or stain.
Blue, yellow, white, and black— All their forms can be seen.
Since all phenomena cannot be borne, One immediately attains the unsurpassed treasure;
In this world, there is no "self" or "person" Who can obtain anything.
Not abiding in the truth of non-abiding, such is the nature of all truths;
that which is realized is without anything seen—such is the truth of the world.
There is no one to cross over and no one not to cross over; at all times in the world, who could exist?
“In the ten directions, those who establish right awakening shall all obtain the unsurpassed treasure.
The Bodhisattva Dharmagatya asked the Tathāgata:
“If one wishes to cause the natural devas and people of the ten directions to all attain their respective places, one should practice the six treasures of the Dharma.”
What are the six kinds of Dharma-treasures?
First, when one hears and knows that this assembly has gathered, this itself is a treasure.
Second, as for the Dharma-treasure: that all those who have come to the assembly hear this sutra, this itself is a treasure.
The Three Dharma Treasures are not merely present merits; they are themselves the treasure.

As for the Four Dharma Treasures, may I venture to ask: although this sutra-dharma has already attained sixty thousand samādhis, it is intended solely to cause the people of the ten directions to give rise to the unsurpassed resolve; thus, it is itself the treasure.
The five Dharma-jewels are those which cause all those in the ten directions to assemble beneath the Bodhi tree; this is the jewel.
The six Dharma-jewels are the sūtras and teachings spoken by the Buddha, which cause all people in the ten directions to obtain them; this is the jewel.

When this samādhi was being preached, there were ninety quadrillion bodhisattvas, devas, humans, and others in the assembly; sixty-seven quadrillion people all attained the state of the non-arising of dharmas.

At that time, nine hundred million bodhisattvas all attained this samādhi. Furthermore, the trichiliocosm Buddha-field shook violently in nine ways. The kings of the thirty-six heavens, remaining in mid-air, played chaotic music and instrumental music to honor the Buddha. All the great nāga kings and asuras likewise beheld this Dharma.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, prostrated himself with his head to the ground, joined his palms in homage to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should I uphold and practice it?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"This is named 'The Infinite Gardens of All Lands with Spontaneous Flowers and Incense,' and it is titled 'The Assembly of Infinite Jewels.'"
When this sutra was being spoken, countless devas, humans, asuras, and non-humans heard the sutra and were all greatly filled with joy; each came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and departed.
